speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these support measures were implemented in a compressed timeline due to the urgency of the situation as well as to achieve timely impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Now that the pandemic has entered a more stabilised phase, can I ask if MOF would be reviewing whether the public spending has been effective in achieving its intended outcomes?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Have the controls and governance procedures been adjusted or waived due to the exigency of the situation?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Are there valuable lessons to learn as to how the Public Service can better manage future crises?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can we be more agile and nimble and how can we achieve better outcomes with the same or less resources?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Without these two schemes, we could have lost capabilities in some sectors of our economy and suffered severe economic scarring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While the economic outlook has improved this year, barring the situation in Eastern Europe, there are still businesses that are directly impacted by the pandemic, such as the tourism and hospitality sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand that the construction sector is also facing challenges of labour crunch, high material and energy costs and snowballing delays among their subcontractors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask if the Government will continue to assist these businesses in 2022?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Are there other targeted support and assistance that we can render these companies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Cash flow is important, especially to small businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whenever there are major event risks, especially, or uncertainties, cash liquidity and credit tend to tighten.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If the interest rates are to rise, as some have forecasted, it could worsen the liquidity situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask if the Government and its purchasing agencies have a policy of paying its vendors in a timely manner?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, in an economically stressed situation, would the Government be even more proactive in making payments to the vendors?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And how can the Government help these suppliers during this difficult period?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are major shifts for businesses and the public to manage, adjust and cope with.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is a whole-of-society effort and also a whole-of-economy undertaking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How and what can MOF agencies, as well as the whole-of-Government do more to help and support businesses and the public in this whole transition?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, in the area of procurement, will the Public Service now have new features in the tender specifications to require vendors or suppliers to achieve the Progressive Wage Mark or to adopt sustainable practices?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The pandemic’s impact on our people made disbursement of funds a top priority, so that citizens and businesses could receive urgent help when it was needed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But we cannot ignore the importance of accountability and governance of public expenditures, in order to ensure that resources are effectively allocated and properly accounted for.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Research carried out by the International Budget Partnership involving 120 countries, found that more than two-thirds of governments had limited or minimal levels of accountability in the introduction and implementation of their early fiscal policy responses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the significant COVID-19-related spending, I would like to call on the Government to subject key COVID-19 expenditures to ex-post analytics and audit checks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In addition, a special audit by the Auditor-General may be warranted to assess procurement processes, including cost reasonableness, taking into consideration the unique market conditions at that time as well as the regularity of transactions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Lastly, the Government drew lower amounts of past reserves for both FY2020 and FY2021 than originally planned.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What lessons can be drawn on the effectiveness and impact of our response to this crisis that can be applied to our management of future ones?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before we raise taxes, we should consider whether there are expenditures we can cut.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is not easy to understand the expenditure in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where is it reflected in the Budget and where and how is the allocation approved?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Explain how the SINGA loans and investments are being treated in the Budget and the Government's statement of assets and liabilities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What does the $2.4 billion recorded as capitalisation of nationally significant infrastructure for FY2022 meet?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I echo the call by the Workers' Party to exempt basic essentials from GST.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To prevent the rich from also benefiting from such exemptions, we can set the price threshold.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NTUC FairPrice house-brand rice sells for $1.40 per kilogram.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can, therefore, exempt rice that sells for, say, under $2 per kilogram from GST.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This way, we prevent luxury goods from being included in the exemption.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Finance Minister let us know how much cost is involved here?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we believe that, in principle, basic necessities should be exempted to help the lower-income households, then, as Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said two days ago when talking about the Ukraine war, we must be prepared to pay the cost for what we believe in.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, what does the Finance Minister expect the GST rate to be in 2030?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Finance Minister said earlier in his round-up speech that my example on land sales is simplistic because land sales will not stay stagnant every year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to clarify that this is only an assumption made for the purpose of simplifying the illustration of the revenue stream.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Varying land sales each year would result in a varying revenue stream but would, in no way, invalidate the model.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure the Finance Minister is able to extrapolate from that illustration what are the variations that would result from a varying land sale.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore will not be pressured to sell more land in order to generate more revenue in bad times.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because the revenue for each year is the accumulation of land sales over many years in the past and the latest year's land sale would have a small impact on the revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, suppose Year 10 is a recessionary year and land sale is only $50 instead of $100, then revenue generated from the land sale in Year 10 is $2.50 instead of $5.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, revenue from previous years' land sales remains unchanged so that the total revenue for the year is $47.5 instead of $50.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A 50% drop in land sale proceeds results in only a 5% drop in revenue because it is cushioned by the land sales in earlier years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conversely, any attempt to sell more land in any particular year would also have limited impact on the revenue for the year since it is spread out over many years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, a rather stable revenue stream.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By "repeatedly", I mean when the lease ends.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And does the same apply to JTC with respect to industrial land?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Our social and healthcare needs will increase while the resources required to support it will be increasingly limited.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the alternative options being considered other than GST that can generate the same revenue to finance the recurrent costs of healthcare and social services?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am dismayed that the Government will be going ahead with the rise in GST.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My main concern is with the impact on the lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note the Government’s explanation that assistance will be provided to this segment of society via various schemes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, I believe any additional cost-cutting measures will be much appreciated by our low-income families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I recall that when Mr Low Thia Khiang raised this issue, the Government had explained that the GST and WCT served different purposes and that applying a value-added tax on water tariffs was standard practice elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We are already taxing our citizens on their water usage via WCT.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is there really a need to perform a double taxation on them with the GST as well?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe Members can agree that there is still a substantial number of low-income Singaporeans, especially those living in HDB’s public rental flats, who are struggling with their utility bills even though they are being assisted with U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: WCT’s amount may seem negligible to many but, to low-income families, every cent and dollar counts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite sluggish demand brought on by the pandemic, our taxi and ride hail ground have told us that their business costs have risen considerably over the past 24 months.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the words of our National Taxi Association President, Brother Raymond Ong, “It is really frightening”.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other cost items that have gone up significantly, some as much as 20%, include the cost of car washes, parking, ERP, signalling a permanent change in their business cost structures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While our drivers appreciate the need for GST increases, our ground has also brought up concerns that they are not GST agents and, undoubtedly, the impending rise will impact their business costs and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, I would like to call for the Ministry to reassess the current expense ratio in calculating our drivers’ taxable incomes and to ask the Ministry for support to be specifically given to our taxi and ride hail drivers in the upcoming GST increase.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore’s infrastructure development and public administration have been pivotal to Singapore’s economic transformation from a Third-World to a First-World country in the last half a century.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This is to fund new rail lines, water and sewerage infrastructure as well as coastal protection measures against rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Experts have highlighted that some of the most significant risks in infrastructure projects lie in scoping, design and cost management as well as project management.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Just last year, the Auditor-General's Office reported lapses in the People’s Association’s development projects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: How does the Government ensure that spending on infrastructure projects consistently offers Singapore value-for-money and is optimised on a lifecycle basis?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Infrastructure and construction technology has made substantial progress over the last decade and continues to do so.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Construction methods, aided by better technology and materials, can improve built costs as well as increase their useable lifespan.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In certain circumstances, a higher initial capital outlay may result in lowering operating costs, which, in turn, contribute to a lower lifecycle cost.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, how does the Government ensure that our expenditure will deliver us the best value over its entire lifecycle?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I will speak on three areas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, one aspect that could be looked at is spending on better materials which will ensure better quality and longer lasting infrastructure; and technologies which will ensure better maintenance productivity, allowing workers to focus on higher value works.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These workers can be retrained in new skillsets that lead to higher productivity and wages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The initial capital outlay may be higher, but the lower operating cost can compensate for that.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, an ACMV system can be a contract for service to the Government instead of capital purchase of the full system.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such changes in procurement strategy can, potentially, create more opportunities for market-based green project financing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, it is heartening that the Government continues to support companies that are impacted by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One question I have is how the Ministry ensures that businesses continue to receive timely and targeted support?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, as disruptions in the global supply chain persist, businesses continue to face stresses, such as delays and cash flow challenges in their operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, to this question, I have a few further clarifications to make.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How has the Government, as a major buyer of goods and services, supported its suppliers and service contractors during this challenging period?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are there any means the Government can ensure it assesses main contractors’ swiftness of payment to its subcontractors and such assessment of its quality as a paymaster be a key consideration in the procurement contract assessment?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is the mechanism in place to make such an assessment?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, we want to ensure that companies receive timely payments to aid their cash flow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, businesses have suffered reduced earnings, increased business costs and cash flow difficulties as revenue became unpredictable due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Added to this are the global supply chain disruptions which COVID-19 has brought about.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In various countries like China, COVID-19 lockdowns and labour disruptions meant that goods which could be shipped in about two weeks’ time could now take three times longer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 outbreaks on container vessels increased freight times as these vessels were either turned away from ports or subjected to quarantine and other measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We recently had our own episode around the Chinese New Year period where COVID-19 cases amongst SATS staff led to severe delays in cargo processing at Changi Airport.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, as Singapore emerges from the COVID-19 pandemic, Singapore must become stronger economically and socially.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore is well-positioned to become a key carbon service hub.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This can generate new opportunities to create new businesses and jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To do this, Singapore will need a coordinated approach and effort to support the transition of businesses to become more sustainable and to take advantage of the opportunities presented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Policy, infrastructure, connections, know-how, innovations and support are needed for businesses to participate and make the transition to a more sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A business ecosystem to support environmental sustainability and inclusive growth will not only help grow our businesses and create good jobs but will improve the environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This benefits the health and quality of life for Singaporeans and protects our environment for future generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: To establish a conducive business ecosystem, it is important to ensure that the regulatory and compliance costs are not prohibitive and are adequate to ensure a reliable and robust system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Above all, these processes must be streamlined and avoid duplicative steps; it must be agile.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their questions and comments for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members' cuts cover four broad topics: first, accountability and governance in our expenditure; second, goods and services tax and other revenue sources; third, support for businesses to overcome COVID-19 disruptions; and last, how we will position our business ecosystem for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The independent, regular and thorough audits by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO) are reported publicly and complemented by Ministries' internal audits as well as their programme evaluation efforts, to ensure that spending translates into good outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ministries are also putting in place enterprise risk management frameworks, which will be reviewed at regular intervals by MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Dedicated function officers have also been set up in MOF to strengthen whole-of-Government processes and capabilities in finance, procurement and grant management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These offices also coordinate across agencies to achieve greater efficiencies and savings in respective functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members of the public have also provided feedback directly to Government agencies on how we can obtain better value from public expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Key Government priorities are monitored regularly and reported in the Annual Budget Book and the biennial Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review (SPOR) report.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The SPOR report was revamped in 2020 to go fully digital and improve accessibility for readers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The content is presented in a more citizen- and business-centric manner, with greater emphasis on outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It highlights the impact on citizens and businesses, such as the fact that one can now start a business within 1.5 days.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Two weeks ago, we published an updated assessment on the impact of key COVID-19 measures, such as the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) and the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The findings show how the Singapore economy has largely avoided medium-term scarring from COVID-19 and is poised to continue its recovery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked about the controls and governance for COVID-19-related schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, as we rolled out COVID-19 schemes quickly, we struck a balance between keeping processes simple and putting in place controls to prevent abuse or errors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For the JSS, a risk assessment is done and, for cases with higher fraud risk, the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) requires firms to authenticate their CPF contributions before releasing payouts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IRAS has denied payments to employers who attempt to abuse the scheme and referred cases to the Police for investigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Despite these efforts, given the unprecedented complexity and the need for urgent disbursement across the board through JSS, there were some mistakes, which are deeply regretted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When such an instance was discovered, we took immediate efforts to rectify them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Edward Chia asked how we ensure value-for-money in major infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before the Government embarks on a project, MOF reviews the project objectives and business case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, at the initial stage, we examine the cost-benefit analysis and consider synergies across projects or other opportunities to optimise resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As the plans develop, MOF works with the development agencies to determine the development approach, design and risk, and use evaluation tools, such as life cycle costing, to optimise costs across the infrastructure lifespan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Edward Chia suggested that we consider buying certain infrastructure or systems as a service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, we are open to such options, which is why life-cycle costing is an important tool to assess different options holistically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For the evaluation of larger and more complex projects, we have benefited from the advice of the Development Projects Advisory Panel, which comprises technical experts from the private sector and academia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But as I have said, we do not just focus on reducing upfront construction costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: By working with agencies on design optimisation and system choices, we seek to reduce total life-cycle costs, which include downstream operating costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As an example, for the Cross Island Line (CRL), LTA is using a different traction power supply system that enables more efficient power transmission.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF also works with development agencies to maintain strong accountability and controls for the management of major infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, to better manage infrastructure project risks, we are consolidating the management of such projects under agencies with stronger expertise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: JTC Corporation, with its deep experience in construction, has helped 28 agencies manage 50 construction projects, worth $9 billion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Sharael Taha's cut asked how much revenue the two-percentage point increase in GST would raise and how much goes towards the offset packages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a clear social purpose in this way of doing things.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The additional $3.5 billion is collected from all, including the rich, foreigners and tourists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The GST Voucher scheme benefits the lower- to middle-income Singaporean households, including most retiree households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is one of the ways we make our system of taxes and transfers a fair and progressive one.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members would remember the chart shown by the Minister for Finance, when we take into account the GSTV and the GST absorbed by the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we achieve this not by exempting certain goods or services for all customers, but by our uniquely Singaporean way of implementing GST with GSTV.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked how we can help private hire car drivers pass on the cost of GST to their commuters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The taxi operators and private hire car platform owners decide on fares.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They may choose to raise fares from time to time, to cover the increase in operating costs and all taxi operators have recently done so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The 60% Fixed Expense Deduction Ratio (FEDR) is set at a level to cover most of the common deductible expenses incurred by drivers in earning their income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In setting the FEDR, we need to strike a balance between simplifying tax compliance and ensuring that it is realistic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The current 60% ratio remains sufficient for the vast majority of drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For those whose actual deductible expenses exceed the 60% ratio, they continue to have the option to file their tax returns based on the actual expenses incurred.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The pandemic continues to disrupt global supply chains and business activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ports and airports around the world today remain affected by pandemic-related restrictions and manpower constraints, resulting in delays and higher transport costs for our businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are aware of the pressures on our businesses and the challenges they face.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has, therefore, continued to provide support to alleviate the impact of the pandemic and made adjustments to changing circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation going into 2022 and adjust our measures as necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, JSS was first designed as a broad-based wage support scheme to help employers retain their local employees when we first began our fight against COVID-19 in 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Payouts were tiered to broadly reflect the different levels of impact on different sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As we went into 2021, some sectors recovered ahead of others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some of our safe management measures had a greater impact on certain sectors, such as construction, F&B, retail, gyms and fitness studios.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, we targeted the JSS to help the sectors most impacted by COVID-19 measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similarly, we acted fast to change the disbursement mode of rental relief from requiring landlords to grant rental waivers, to giving direct payouts to tenants under the Rental Support Scheme (RSS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was possible as 90% of these businesses were registered under PayNow Corporate or had existing GIRO arrangements with IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IRAS combined the data it had across various tax types to auto disburse the RSS payouts directly to more than 80% of eligible tenants and owner-occupants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was the first time the Government gave direct disbursements to tenants and we received positive feedback that the disbursements were fast and effortless.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to invest in capabilities for business grant disbursements, so that our assistance can reach businesses promptly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Edward Chia have observed, our businesses appreciate prompt payment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF has worked on providing faster payments to our suppliers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ease our suppliers' cash flows, we pay our vendors faster by streamlining the procure-to-pay process from procurement, to goods receipt and payment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As at end January 2020, about 97% of e-invoices below $5,000 were paid within 12 days, ahead of the usual credit term of 30 days.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To further ease suppliers' cash flows, we are working with MTI to allow auto-approval for factoring of certain Government contracts later this year, so that our suppliers can have more financing options.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also aware of the challenges faced by Government construction contractors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The pandemic continues to impact the productivity on-site, supply chain and manpower availability, leading to delays and cost increases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has taken a proactive stance to shoulder part of the cost increases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This aims to soften the impact of productivity loss from requirements, such as safe management measures on-site and shortage of foreign manpower due to border controls.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include the costs of prolongation, increased manpower costs and consultancy services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These measures, including support for manpower costs through JSS and foreign worker levy waivers and rebates, have helped our construction suppliers through the crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On Mr Edward Chia's suggestion to assess main contractors payment promptness to subcontractors in our tender evaluation, it is not easy for a service buyer to verify or monitor the private business practices of its contractors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In general, if a contractor does not treat its subcontractor well, we expect few subcontractors would be keen to work with it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where such market forces have not worked so well, the Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment Act provides legal recourse for subcontractors affected by late or no payment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked whether a select group of companies enjoyed outsized windfalls from the COVID-19 support schemes and how these companies can contribute back for the common good.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But to finely target by the fortunes of individual businesses would not be possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When businesses flourish or do exceptionally well, they pay more Corporate Income Tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Their workers who receive bonuses also pay taxes, including GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such additional revenue can then be channelled to fund Government programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some businesses have also taken the initiative to contribute to the community in various ways through their corporate social responsibility activities, which is commendable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Moving from businesses to families, let me address Ms Mariam Jaafar’s question of how we reach out to vulnerable individuals and families without their own homes when many support measures are tied to the household or housing type.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Government assistance is prioritised for families with less means and in greater need of social support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In means-testing for our social schemes, housing type is one of the proxies we use to estimate an individual’s means.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also look at other factors, such as income and number of members in the household.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A person living in a higher value property or larger housing type is, in general, more likely to have access to resources or support through the family.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where there are exceptional circumstances, I encourage our Members of Parliament and community leaders to bring these cases to the attention of the relevant agencies so that their circumstances can be holistically assessed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will elaborate on how we are stepping up our efforts in two areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we will strengthen Singapore as a trusted, open and effective business hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to enhance our corporate governance regime to combat money laundering, terrorism financing and other threats to the integrity of the international financial system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes aligning ourselves with international standards, such as those under the intergovernmental Financial Action Task Force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, in January this year, Parliament passed the Corporate Registers (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill to strengthen Singapore’s regime on the transparency and beneficial ownership of companies and Limited Liability Partnerships.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA is pivoting towards more risk-targeted supervision for the Registered Filing Agents sector by using data analytics to identify higher-risk agents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is also studying proposals to further enhance our anti-money laundering regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will consult the public on these proposals later in the year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Apart from our work to combat money laundering, we are also strengthening Singapore’s position as a global Intellectual Property (IP) hub, as well as a fund management hub by ensuring that the regulatory framework keeps pace with business needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we will work with businesses to improve the efficiency of processes, such as tax filing, payments and trade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For tax filing, IRAS collaborates with software developers and other Government agencies to develop solutions to help businesses to meet their tax and other regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Businesses which adopt software listed on IRAS’ new Accounting Software Register Plus can now seamlessly submit their tax returns and transact with their business partners on the InvoiceNow network.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For payments, IRAS introduced PayNow for corporate income tax (CIT) refunds last year, so that businesses can enjoy fast, secure and seamless e-refunds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Taxpayers would be updated by their banks when the refunds have been credited into their bank accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, all businesses that are due to receive CIT refunds from IRAS can choose between GIRO and PayNow to receive their refunds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For trade processes, Singapore Customs has digitalised banker’s guarantees for traders through the Networked Trade Platform (NTP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Traders do not need to physically collect and submit paper guarantees, as participating banks can send e-guarantees data to Customs securely through the NTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Almost 90% of all guarantees issued by the six participating banks last year were e-guarantees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I am heartened that Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Jessica Tan have asked about our initiatives to enhance our business ecosystem to support environmental sustainability and inclusive growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has been playing its part as a socially-responsible and environmentally-conscious buyer and encourages businesses to do the same.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, our suppliers for security, cleaning, lift maintenance and landscaping are already required to pay progressive wages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOM will share more on progressive wages in their COS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have been incorporating sustainability requirements in our tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, all new Government buildings and premises undergoing major renovations are required to meet stringent Green Mark standards under the GreenGov.SG initiative.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have also been buying green products, such as printing paper, that are accredited with the Singapore Green Label.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The latest demand aggregation tender for vehicle hiring services includes hybrid vehicles as part of the requirements and incorporates clauses to provide for electric vehicles when they become more prevalent in future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to expand the list of buys where green requirements are incorporated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also consider the sustainability credentials of suppliers during the evaluation for Government tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In construction, the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) requires contractors to adopt environmental management practices before they can be registered to undertake building or civil engineering works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In addition, agencies like LTA and JTC have included environmental sustainability criteria in their construction tenders that give extra points to suppliers that have adopted green practices or obtained green awards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The consideration of sustainability credentials will be extended to the procurement of more categories of goods and services and was recently piloted in tenders for public waste collection and accommodation and event venues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To enable the transition towards sustainability, the Government has been supporting businesses in going green and welcomes businesses to make use of the support available.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes schemes, such as Enterprise Singapore’s Enterprise Sustainability Programme, the Economic Development Board’s Resource Efficiency Grant for Energy and the National Environment Agency’s Energy Efficiency Fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Enterprise Sustainability Programme, the Government shares the risk with banks in lending to businesses to develop innovative green technologies and solutions, such as in clean energy and the circular economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: BCA has also introduced various Green Mark Incentive Schemes to encourage the adoption of environmentally-friendly building technologies and building design practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He asked if we could abolish GST on the Water Conservation Tax (WCT).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Workers' Party had asked this before and the Government had explained it previously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The WCT is how we have been able to make our water supply more resilient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With the threat of climate change, water resilience is more important than ever.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The WCT reflects the fact that water is precious and encourages every individual and business to play a role in conserving our water resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The water tariff and WCT together form the final price of water, reflecting the economic cost of producing water from our desalination and NEWater plants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: GST is then levied on this final price, inclusive of taxes and duties that are related to the supply of goods or services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This approach is consistent with the practice in other jurisdictions, such as the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If I may understand Mr Faisal Manap's concern, it is really for the lower-income households and the fact that they would have to pay GST on the water conservation tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first point I would make is that the amount is low.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But, more importantly, with the U-Save rebates and vouchers that have been given, these households will, actually, be able to cover their utilities bills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, they need not worry and Mr Faisal Manap should reassure his residents that, with the U-Save rebates that are given from the Government, they will be well taken care of by this Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, please, I would encourage Mr Faisal Manap to visit the MOF website.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The infographics are there, setting out the various archetypes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Please print them and please distribute them freely to your residents, especially to the lower-income households, and reassure them that this Government will take care of them as far as that is concerned and they need not be worried about the water conservation tax, or the GST thereon.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Hazel Poa had a couple of questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Her question was about the additional costs that would be incurred.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Her question was premised on, if we believe that basic necessities should be exempt, what should be done about this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I just would like to point out to Ms Hazel Poa that the underlying premise of her question was, if we believe that basic necessities should be exempt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And there is a philosophical difference between what PSP believes and what this Government believes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I do not think that it would be very helpful to go into the details of the question because it is premised on assuming an approach to basic necessities that we have a fundamental difference on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The same would apply to her question on land sales.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think she had an elaborate example, but going into the details or discussing the minutiae or the technical details of that is not really going to take us much further.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In its physical form, it is an asset, it has a value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If you sell it, it gets converted into cash, but we put it back into the reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some of it comes back in the form of the NIRC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Selling it and stretching it out over 10 years, 30 years, 99 years, fundamentally, is still a departure from the principle that we adhere to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, all I would say here is that it was comprehensively answered by the Finance Minister earlier and I do not think it is necessary for me to elaborate further on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai had a question on how we account for large expenditures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is to allow the public to understand the major categories of Government spending, such as Expenditure on Manpower, Other Operating Expenditure, Grants and Transfers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, if he looks into the Budget Book for examples of COVID-19 spending, at page 55, under MSF's operating expenditure, there will be a reference to the extension of the COVID-19 Recovery Grant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If he looks at a different Ministry, let us, say, MOF, page 95, he will see that, under the fifth paragraph, there is a reference there to COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What I am trying to illustrate is that, for accountability purposes, it is set out according to Heads of Expenditure, that is the various Ministries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Within the various Heads, if you are looking for a particular large expenditure like COVID-19, there will be a reference to COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That said, we are always open to seeing how things can be presented better or in a way that is more intuitive and we will take that into account.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think he had some other questions on SINGA, but that was extensively debated earlier in the year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some questions in relation to MAS, that would be publicly available as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The thing is this, if Mr Leong Mun Wai would like very specific figures or specific data, the better way to do that would be to file a Parliamentary Question (PQ) and then we would have the appropriate time to look for the specific answer that he needs and to address this concern.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think I have covered most of the questions, Mr Chairman.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is one clarification if that can be done.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think this needs to be another PQ.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, if it is something that is already publicly available, then I do not need to confirm it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if it is something that he wishes confirmation on, then I will have to check it, because if I were to give confirmation on anything, I would like to be sure that it is actually correct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if the Member would just let me have that, drop me a note or he could file a Parliamentary Question (PQ), we will see how best to address it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the other point about the expenditures, we will look and see how we can present this in a manner that is useful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I say this because I do not want to leave the Member with an impression that MOF will always be collating and organising information at individual Member's request because that is very difficult to do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we do understand that the public wants to understand how certain figures and expenditures are dealt with and we will see how we can do that in a meaningful way.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Apart from the two questions that the Minister feels is not necessary to answer, I have a few other questions mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sorry, the last question was whether land will be repeatedly sold to whom?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Do you mean the land for HDB development?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: At the end of the lease, when it returns to the Government, will it again, you know, repeat?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, that would happen once every 99 years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we have not quite reached that stage yet and it might be a little premature to address that question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, we really do not know at this point of time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, we will try to make that last as long as we possibly can with the revenues that we have.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think the last question was, what would be the tax rate increase?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not have that figure with me at the moment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Perhaps if the Member just files a PQ on that, I will get back to her.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I am asking her to confirm that number.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is it a number that cannot be confirmed?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or I do not know what is the reason why it cannot be spoken in Parliament?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Leong Mun Wai's faith in my abilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I do not usually carry all the figures of all published Government data in my head.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if Mr Leong Mun Wai is saying that there is a figure which is out there and it is published, and it is published by a Government agency, then I would have to assume that it is correct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just that if I do not have the figure with me at the moment and if it is MAS – because he must remember that I am with MOF – I would like to check before I give any confirmations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If he has an issue with the figure, he should let us know what the problem is as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, he is asking about a figure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If it is published and it is a published figure from the Government, he can take it that that is the figure.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No, Chairman, if there is a question, I have to ask the question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if there is a time limit, we cannot ask any more questions, even though those are relevant questions?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to, firstly, congratulate the Finance Minister for his maiden Budget, which is very well-structured and far-reaching; and also to thank the Second Minister for Finance for answering our questions as well as the MOF team for the tremendous work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I hope that FY 2022/2023 will be a one-Budget FY, which will mean that we are back to a normalised or stable environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Nevertheless, I am sure Members in this House would be ready to consider any additional fiscal measures should the situation deteriorate and the need arises to support Singaporean families, households and businesses as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: With that, Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw the amendment.
